newsitem.title: DUBAI: Most Arabs denounce U.S. strike on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Most Arabs denounce U.S. strike on Iraq.

text.p: Much of the Arab world condemned Tuesday's U.S. missile attack on Iraq as infringing an Arab country's sovereignty and some said it would only raise tension and instability in the Middle East.
Kuwait, Iraq's small southern neighbour occupied by Baghdad in 1990-91, said it fully understood the U.S. attack.

But Iraq's other Gulf Arab neighbours, including Washington's key Arab ally Saudi Arabia, remained silent hours after U.S. forces retaliated for last weekend's Iraqi attacks in support of a Kurdish faction fighting another Kurdish group in northern Iraq.
"The Arab League Secretary General, Esmat Abdel-Meguid, deeply renounced the attack, which does not rely upon any international legitimacy," the Arab League said in a statement.
"It is thus considered an infringement of an Arab country's sovereignty...and an interference in its internal affairs."

The Cairo-based league -- which groups all 22 Arab countries but does not alway reflect unified policies of all its members -- said the cruise missile attack by the U.S. warships and B-52 bombers against air defence and communications targets in southern Iraq also contradicted international law.
"The use of military force will lead only to more aggravation in the situation and expose the region to factors of tension and instability," it added.

An Egyptian foreign ministry spokesman said: "Egypt is following with deep concern the current incidents on the Iraqi land and accompanied military movements and the use of force in north and south Iraq, increasing tension inside Iraq and the region and threatening civilian lives."
"Egypt underlines the importance of principles and goals of the U.N. charter, which guarantee Iraq's sovereignty, integrity and non-interference in its internal affairs," he added.

In Syria, which for years has been at odds with Iraqi President Saddam Hussein, there was no immediate reaction, but hours before the U.S. strike Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara said Syria opposed any interference in the affairs of Iraq.
There was no reaction from Saudi Arabia and most other Gulf Arab states, which cut ties with Iraq over its 1990 invasion of Kuwait and took part in the allied liberation.
The Gulf Arabs had previously supported action against Iraq when it threatened their security.
Kuwait, expressed "full understanding" for the attack, the official news agency KUNA said.
"Kuwait reaffirms the necessity of Iraq's full compliance with all international resolutions to ensure peace and stability in the region," a cabinet statement said.
Jordan on Tuesday expressed concern over the attack and called for restraint to avoid a further escalation of violence.

"Jordan is following with concern the latest escalation in the situation and the military operations which might return Iraq to the cycle of violence and counter-violence," Information Minister Marwan Muasher told reporters.
Palestinian officials denounced the attack as unjustified and said Iraq was entitled to protect its borders.
